title: Why Christians will not rank Jesus with Apollo or Zeus
source_text: Αἰγύπτιοι μὲν οὖν διδαχθέντες τὸν Ἀντίνουν σέβειν, ἐὰν παραβάλῃς (αὐτῷ) Ἀπόλλωνα ἢ Δία, ἀνέξονται, σεμνύνοντες τὸν Ἀντίνουν διὰ τοῦ ἐκείνοις αὐτὸν συναριθμεῖν· καὶ ἐν τούτοις γὰρ ὁ Κέλσος σαφῶς ψεύδεται λέγων· κἂν παραβάλῃς αὐτῷ τὸν Ἀπόλλωνα ἢ τὸν Δία, οὐκ ἀνέξονται. Χριστιανοῖς δὲ μεμαθηκόσι τὴν αἰώνιον αὐτοῖς εἶναι ζωὴν ἐν τῷ γινώσκειν „τὸν μόνον“ ἐπὶ πᾶσιν „ἀληθινὸν θεὸν καὶ ὃν“ ἐκεῖνος ἀπέστειλεν „Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν,“ μαθοῦσι δὲ καὶ „ὅτι πάντες μὲν οἱ θεοὶ τῶν ἐθνῶν εἰσι δαιμόνια“ λίχνα καὶ περὶ τὰς θυσίας καὶ τὰ αἵματα καὶ τὰς ἀπὸ τῶν θυσιῶν ἀποφορὰς καλινδούμενα ἐπὶ ἀπάτῃ τῶν μὴ προσπεφευγότων τῷ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεῷ, οἱ δὲ τοῦ θεοῦ θεῖοι καὶ ἅγιοι ἄγγελοι ἄλλης εἰσὶ φύσεως καὶ προαιρέσεως παρὰ τοὺς ἐπὶ γῆς πάντας δαίμονας, καὶ ὅτι οὗτοι σφόδρα ὀλίγοις γινώσκονται τοῖς περὶ τῶν τοιούτων συνετῶς καὶ ἐπιμελῶς ζητήσασιν, ἐὰν παραβάλῃς Ἀπόλλωνα καὶ Δία ἤ τινα τῶν μετὰ κνίσσης καὶ αἵματος καὶ θυσιῶν προσκυνουμένων, οὐκ ἀνέξονται· τινὲς μὲν διὰ τὴν πολλὴν ἁπλότητα μὴ εἰδότες μὲν δοῦναι λόγον περὶ ὧν ποιοῦσιν εὐγνωμόνως δὲ τηροῦντες ἃ παρειλήφασιν, ἕτεροι δὲ μετ᾿ οὐκ εὐκαταφρονήτων λόγων ἀλλὰ καὶ βαθυτέρων καὶ, ὡς ἂν εἴποι τις Ἕλλην, ἐσωτερικῶν καὶ ἐποπτικῶν, ἐν οἷς πολύς ἐστι λόγος περὶ θεοῦ καὶ τῶν τετιμημένων ἀπὸ θεοῦ διὰ τοῦ μονογενοῦς θεοῦ λόγου μετοχῇ θεότητος διὰ τοῦτο δὲ καὶ ὀνόματι. πολὺς δὲ ὁ λόγος καὶ ὁ περὶ τῶν θείων ἀγγέλων καὶ ὁ περὶ τῶν ἐναντίων μὲν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ ἠπατημένων δὲ καὶ ἐξ ἀπάτης αὐτοὺς ἀναγορευόντων θεοὺς ἢ ἀγγέλους θεοῦ ἢ δαίμονας ἀγαθοὺς ἢ ἥρωας ἐκ μεταβολῆς συστάντας ἀγαθῆς ἀνθρωπίνης ψυχῆς. οἱ δὲ τοιοῦτοι Χριστιανοὶ εἶναι ἐν ἀληθείᾳ, ἤτοι ἑαυτοὺς ὥσπερ πολλοὶ ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ δοκοῦσιν εἶναι ἐν ἀληθείᾳ, ἤτοι ἑαυτοὺς κατασοφισάμενοι λόγοις πιθανοῖς ἢ τοῖς ὑφ᾿ ἑτέρων προσαγομένοις καὶ εὑρεθεῖσι συγκαταθέμενοι προπετῶς, οὕτως εἰσὶ καὶ [αἱ] ἐν ταῖς ἔξω σωμάτων ψυχαῖς καὶ ἀγγέλοις καὶ δαίμοσί τινες, ὑπὸ τῶν πιθανοτήτων ἑλκυσθέντες πρὸς τὸ ἑαυτοὺς ἀναγορεῦσαι θεούς. καὶ διὰ τοὺς τοιούτους γε λόγους κατὰ τὸ ἀκριβὲς τελείως ἐν ἀνθρώποις μὴ δυναμένους εὑρεθῆναι ἀσφαλὲς ἐνομίσθη τὸ μηδενὶ ἑαυτὸν ἐμπιστεῦσαι ἄνθρωπον ὄντα ὡς θεῷ, πλὴν μόνου τοῦ ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ὡς διαιτητοῦ, τοῦ βαθύτατα ταῦτα καὶ θεωρήσαντος καὶ ὀλίγοις παραδόντος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.
pass_a_gloss: Egyptians (Αἰγύπτιοι) then, taught (διδάσκω) to worship (σέβειν) Antinous, if you compare (παραβάλλω) Apollo or Zeus [to him], will tolerate it (ἀνέχομαι), exalting (σεμνύνω) Antinous by numbering him with (συναριθμέω) those; for in these things too Celsus plainly lies (ψεύδεται), saying: 'even if you compare to him Apollo or Zeus, they will not tolerate it.' But Christians, having learned that eternal life (αἰώνιος ζωή) is for them in knowing (γινώσκω) 'the only' over-all 'true God and whom' he sent 'Jesus Christ' [John 17:3], and having learned 'that all the gods of the nations are demons (δαιμόνια)' [LXX Ps 95:5] greedy/gluttonous (λίχνος), rolling about (καλινδέομαι) around sacrifices (θυσίαι), blood (αἷμα), and offerings carried off (ἀποφοραί) from sacrifices, for deception (ἀπάτη) of those not having fled for refuge (προσφεύγω) to the God over all; and that God's divine and holy angels (ἄγγελοι) are of another nature (φύσις) and choice/will (προαίρεσις) than all the demons on earth, and that these are known to very few who have searched (ζητέω) about such things with understanding (συνετῶς) and care (ἐπιμελῶς): if you compare Apollo and Zeus or any of those worshipped (προσκυνέω) with savour of fat (κνῖσα), blood, and sacrifices, they will not tolerate it; some through much simplicity (ἁπλότης) not knowing how to give an account (λόγον δοῦναι) of what they do, but keeping (τηρέω) sensibly/fair-mindedly (εὐγνωμόνως) what they received (παραλαμβάνω); others with not contemptible (εὐκαταφρόνητος) arguments but deeper (βαθύτερος) and, as a Greek might say, esoteric (ἐσωτερικός) and epoptic (ἐποπτικός, of the highest initiation), in which there is much discourse about God and those honoured (τιμάω) by God through the only-begotten God the Word (μονογενὴς θεὸς λόγος) by participation (μετοχή) in deity (θεότης), and therefore also in the name (ὄνομα). Much discourse also about the divine angels and about those opposed (ἐναντίος) to the truth but deceived (ἀπατάω), and from deception proclaiming (ἀναγορεύω) themselves gods or angels of God or good demons or heroes (ἥρωες) constituted (συνίστημι) from the change (μεταβολή) of a good human soul. [Staged text here has a garbled clause: 'such ones Christians to be in truth, either themselves' — not construable; see notes.] As many in philosophy (φιλοσοφία) think to be in the truth, either having out-sophisticated themselves (κατασοφίζομαι) by persuasive arguments (λόγοι πιθανοί) or having rashly (προπετῶς) assented (συγκατατίθεμαι) to those brought forward and found by others, so also among souls outside bodies (ἔξω σωμάτων ψυχαί), angels, and demons there are some drawn (ἕλκω) by plausibilities (πιθανότητες) to proclaim themselves gods. And because of such arguments/questions not able to be found perfectly with exactness (κατὰ τὸ ἀκριβές) among men, it was thought safe (ἀσφαλές) for one being a man to entrust (ἐμπιστεύω) himself to no one as to God, except only the one over all, as arbiter (διαιτητής) [having] the one who most deeply contemplated (θεωρέω) these things and handed them (παραδίδωμι) to few, Jesus Christ.
pass_b_english: The Egyptians, then, who have been taught to worship Antinous, will put up with it if you set Apollo or Zeus beside him, for they exalt Antinous by counting him among those gods. For here too Celsus plainly lies when he says, “Even if you set Apollo or Zeus beside him, they will not put up with it.”

But Christians have learned that their eternal life lies in knowing “the only true God,” who is over all, “and Jesus Christ, whom” he “has sent” (John 17:3). They have learned too “that all the gods of the nations are demons” (Psalm 96:5), greedy demons that wallow about the sacrifices, the blood, and the portions taken from the sacrifices, to deceive those who have not fled for refuge to the God who is over all; while the divine and holy angels of God are of another nature and another will than all the demons on earth, and are known to very few, to those who have searched into such things with understanding and care. If you set beside him Apollo and Zeus, or any of those worshipped with the savour of burnt fat, with blood, and with sacrifices, Christians will not put up with it. Some of them, in their great simplicity, do not know how to give an account of what they do, but sensibly keep what they have received. Others refuse with arguments that are not to be despised, arguments that are deeper and, as a Greek might say, esoteric and fit for those who have seen the higher mysteries. In these there is much discussion of God, and of those whom God, through the only-begotten God the Word, has honoured with a share in deity, and for that reason with the name as well. There is much discussion too of the divine angels, and of those who are opposed to the truth yet have themselves been deceived, and who out of that deception proclaim themselves gods, or angels of God, or good demons, or heroes formed by the change of a good human soul.

For just as many in philosophy suppose that they are in the truth, either because they have deceived themselves with plausible arguments or because they have rashly assented to arguments that others have put forward and devised, so too among souls outside bodies, and among angels and demons, there are some who have been drawn by plausible reasonings into proclaiming themselves gods. And because such questions cannot be found out among men with complete exactness, it has been judged safe for one who is a man to entrust himself to no one as to God except to the God who is over all alone, with Jesus Christ as arbiter, who looked most deeply into these things and handed them on to a few.

choices.choice: Copy-text: staged source_3.json section 37 (Koetschau 3.37); checked against the local Perseus TEI (origen_celsum.xml), which has the same wording. Psalm: Origen quotes LXX Psalm 95:5 (ὅτι πάντες οἱ θεοὶ τῶν ἐθνῶν δαιμόνια), which is Psalm 96:5 in English Bibles; the following adjective λίχνα and the rest of that clause are Origen's own expansion, not part of the verse, so the quotation marks close after 'demons'. John 17:3 is quoted with Origen's own insertions (ἐπὶ πᾶσιν 'over all', ἐκεῖνος 'he'), which are kept outside the quotation marks. Celsus's quoted sentence ('Even if you set Apollo or Zeus beside him, they will not put up with it') was said of the Egyptians; Origen calls it a lie about them and then turns it to the Christians. DOUBTFUL READING: the staged text and the TEI both read 'οἱ δὲ τοιοῦτοι Χριστιανοὶ εἶναι ἐν ἀληθείᾳ, ἤτοι ἑαυτοὺς ὥσπερ πολλοὶ ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ δοκοῦσιν εἶναι ἐν ἀληθείᾳ, ἤτοι ἑαυτοὺς κατασοφισάμενοι…'. The opening words ('such ones … Christians to be in truth, either themselves') cannot be construed and look like a digitising error (a garbled line or dittography of the following line); the translation follows the coherent sentence 'ὥσπερ πολλοὶ … οὕτως εἰσὶ καί…' and leaves the stray words out. This must be checked against the printed Koetschau page (GCS 2, p. 70; TEI alt page 471-472) before certification. [αἱ] is bracketed by the editor and not translated. 'Through the only-begotten God the Word' (διὰ τοῦ μονογενοῦς θεοῦ λόγου) echoes John 1:18 (μονογενὴς θεός) and the gift of the name 'gods' may glance at Psalm 82:6 (LXX 81:6) and John 10:34-35; both are possible allusions only and are not cited inline. Syntax of the last clause is ambiguous: πλὴν μόνου τοῦ ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ὡς διαιτητοῦ, τοῦ … Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ is taken as 'except the God over all, with Jesus Christ as arbiter'; an alternative reading takes διαιτητοῦ with τοῦ ἐπὶ πᾶσιν. ἐποπτικῶν is rendered 'fit for those who have seen the higher mysteries' (the epoptic grade of the Eleusinian rites). δαιμόνια/δαίμονες are rendered 'demons' throughout, following the house usage in this work; 'good demons' renders the pagan phrase δαίμονας ἀγαθούς.
kept γάρ: 'For here too Celsus plainly lies'
προσπεφευγότων: 'fled for refuge to' (was 'taken refuge with')
kept the μέν/δέ contrast: 'opposed to the truth yet have themselves been deceived'
checked John 17:3 (Origen's insertions outside the quotation marks) and LXX Psalm 95:5 = Psalm 96:5; both correct

The staged text and the Perseus TEI (origen_celsum.xml line 6157) both read 'οἱ δὲ τοιοῦτοι Χριστιανοὶ εἶναι ἐν ἀληθείᾳ, ἤτοι ἑαυτοὺς' before 'ὥσπερ πολλοὶ'. It cannot be construed and looks like a duplicated line, so the translation leaves it out. Confirm against the printed Koetschau page (GCS 2, p. 70) before certifying.
